overview: The western Frankish kingdom continued through struggles among royal families and regional powers. This entry’s 900 to 1000 coverage includes both late Carolingian kings and Hugh Capet’s accession in 987. Monastery documents, manuscripts and excavated villages reveal lives that cannot be reduced to a sequence of kings.

periods.title: Late Carolingian kings and rivals
periods.summary: Carolingian rulers competed with other leading families. Louis IV returned from English exile in 936 to become king.

periods.title: The first Capetian generation
periods.summary: Hugh Capet’s election in 987 changed the ruling dynasty. The kingdom continued beyond the imported map interval.

items.text: In 923 Queen Eadgifu took her young son Louis to England after his father lost power. He returned in 936 as King Louis IV. His childhood illustrates how royal family connections could provide refuge during political crises, and how a future king might grow up far from his kingdom.

At Saint-Gilles de Missignac near Aimargues, excavation revealed a village with a particularly active phase between the ninth and eleventh centuries. Houses, paths, courtyards, a church and a cemetery show a lived landscape. This southern village provides a local example, not a model of every western Frankish settlement.

Missignac’s excavated houses were often built of earth, with one or two rooms; archaeologists suggest upper spaces sometimes stored hay or grain. Some buildings used stone bases and tiles. These observations come from a settlement occupied over centuries, so the surviving plan should not be read as one frozen moment.

Archaeologists identified about 450 grain-storage pits across Missignac’s occupation. They did not all operate at once. A large archaeological total can represent generations of storage and replacement: it does not mean one extraordinarily hungry family had 450 pantries.

Finds at Missignac include weaving weights, sickles and milling stones, linking household life with cloth production, harvesting and grinding grain. Some abandoned storage pits later received rubbish. The objects preserve traces of work even where written records do not tell us who performed it.

When William founded Cluny around 910, his gift included a rural estate with resources such as vineyards, meadows, woods, mills and ponds. A monastery required a working economic base. Prayer might organize its day, but food and maintenance still had to come from somewhere.

Cluny’s foundation arranged for its community to choose later abbots after Berno, its first leader, and placed the house under papal protection. These provisions shaped who could control the institution. They describe this monastery’s legal arrangements rather than independence from every outside pressure.

In 931 Abbot Odo received papal authorization to reform other monasteries that wished to adopt Cluny’s observance. The community’s influence could therefore extend through practices and institutional connections. The enormous later medieval church at Cluny should not be projected backward into this early foundation.

Gerbert taught at Reims from the 970s after earlier study in Catalonia. His career linked learning in different regions, and he later became Pope Sylvester II in 999. Mathematics and teaching formed part of this story alongside church politics.

Evidence for Gerbert’s mathematics includes a letter explaining place-value multiplication and Richer’s description of an abacus with twenty-seven columns. Moving a counter between columns changes its value. Modern classroom reconstructions can illustrate the principle, but their added colors or teaching tricks are not automatically medieval evidence.

A surviving Romance oath begins “Pro Deo amur et pro christian poblo”: “For the love of God and for the Christian people.” It belongs to the Strasbourg alliance of 842, before this map interval. The wording offers a brief glimpse of written speech distinct from the Latin framing narrative.

The Strasbourg oaths are preserved in Nithard’s history through a manuscript copied in the late tenth or early eleventh century, now BnF Latin 9768. It is not a signed document from the 842 ceremony. The dates of an event, its composition and a surviving copy can differ substantially.

Carolingian coins of the eighth through tenth centuries were mostly silver. Their designs could include crosses, royal monograms, temple forms and mint names. Such small objects joined writing, authority and exchange; finding a coin does not establish that every household transaction used money.

ending.text: Hugh Capet’s election in 987 ended the sequence of western Carolingian kings and began a new dynasty. The kingdom continued. Its people, villages and institutions did not vanish at that change or at the map’s 1000 endpoint.
